metadata.title: Family-supported hearing aid use behaviour intervention to improve outcomes in older adults at high risk for dementia (SOUND): study protocol for a randomised controlled trial

sections.text: Abstract Background Hearing loss (HL) imposes a substantial burden on families and society and is the largest modifiable risk factor for dementia. As a practical and non-invasive approach to managing HL, hearing aid use has been associated with a reduced risk of incident dementia and global cognitive decline. However, high-level evidence on the cognitive benefits of hearing aids among those at high dementia risk is scarce and adherence to hearing aid use remains challenging. Our study aims to explore whether a family-supported hearing aid use behaviour intervention, guided by the integrated framework of self-determination theory, technology acceptance model and family social support theory, can improve cognitive function in Chinese older adults with both HL and mild cognitive impairment (MCI). Methods and analysis This study is a two-arm, single-blinded, randomised controlled trial. A total of 150 participants with HL and MCI will be randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio to either an intervention group (hearing aid use and family intervention) or a control group (hearing aid use and regular health education). All interventions will last for 4 months. Hearing aid use will be delivered by professional audiologists, while family caregivers will deliver the behavioural intervention at home after receiving standardised training from researchers and guidance through structured manuals. Furthermore, family caregivers will be guided through a WeChat group to address unresolved issues related to hearing aid maintenance and intervention skills. The primary outcome is cognitive function measured by the Montreal Cognitive Assessment–Hearing Impairment at baseline and follow-up. Secondary outcomes include adherence score to hearing aid use measured by daily duration and weekly frequency, hearing aid use skills, motivation, activities of daily life, quality of life, depressive symptoms, subjective cognitive decline, social support, self-efficacy, healthcare utilisation, autonomy support and caregiver burden. Ethics and dissemination The study was approved by the Institutional Review Board of Peking University. Research findings will be published in peer-reviewed journals and at national and international conferences. Trial registration number ChiCTR2400091791.

Hearing loss (HL) is one of the largest modifiable risk factors for dementia, 1 potentially affecting cognitive function through excessive cognitive load, brain structure changes and reduced social engagement. 2 The Lancet Commission report has estimated that prevention of HL could reduce dementia cases by 7%. 1 Accumulating evidence has also suggested that older adults with HL have a 1.44 to 2.06 times higher risk for mild cognitive impairment (MCI), 3 as well as a 1.28 to 2.42 times higher risk of developing dementia. 4 Due to no curable medicines or treatments for dementia available currently, 5 exploring interventions for HL is crucial for preventing and delaying the onset of dementia. 6 Using hearing aids is a practical and non-invasive option for managing HL 7 ; however, high-quality evidence regarding their effects on cognitive function remains limited, with only a small number of studies reporting significant benefits. 8 9 Poor adherence to hearing aid use (HAU) may partly explain why some randomised controlled trials (RCTs) have failed to demonstrate improved cognitive performance compared with control groups. 10 11 As an intermediate stage between normal age-associated cognitive deterioration and dementia, MCI received widespread attention in dementia research. 12 Hearing-impaired older adults with MCI remain at greater risk of developing dementia than those without a history of MCI, even though HAU may help reduce the risk of progression from MCI to dementia. 13 Thus, older adults with MCI are commonly regarded as a population at high risk for dementia. 14 However, for this group, maintaining HAU is particularly challenging. Although the Ageing and Cognitive Health Evaluation in Elders RCT found that hearing aids reduced cognitive decline in high-risk older adults with poor hearing, 9 individuals at high risk for dementia often experience greater difficulty using hearing aids because of poorer working memory, impaired executive function and more emotional problems. 15 These difficulties may limit their ability to acquire HAU skills and adapt to the devices, thereby reducing long-term adherence 15 and potentially attenuating the cognitive benefits of HAU. Evidence suggests that individuals with dementia are 2.07 times more likely to discontinue HAU within 1 year of adoption than the general population⁠. 16 Therefore, behavioural interventions to improve adherence to HAU are needed in this high-risk population. Family support is a promising strategy for improving hearing aid adherence, especially for older adults at high risk of dementia with impaired memory and executive function. According to the Family Social Support (FSS) theory, family support is a highly personalised, interactive, and sustainable form of social support, and it presents the primary source of social support for older adults. 17 Family support is also a crucial external support environmental factor. Consistent with this view, several family-related factors, such as marital status and communication needs with family members, have been associated with better adherence to HAU. 18 19 Furthermore, integrating behavioural change theories with the FSS theory may provide a useful framework for designing interventions to improve hearing aid adherence in older adults at high risk for dementia. Self-determination theory (SDT) suggests that a supportive external environment can stimulate autonomous motivation and facilitate the transformation of controlled motivation into autonomous motivation. 20 21 Technology acceptance model (TAM) further highlights the importance of perceptions of electronic services (such as hearing aids) in shaping the attitude, motivation and behaviour of HAU. 22 Hence, the integration of SDT and TAM theories based on FSS theory (SDT-TAM-FSS theory) could focus external supportive environment on family support and improve the autonomous motivation through perception factors of older individuals including perceived observability, perceived compatibility, and perceived ease of use, which may be a potential method to help older adults at high risk for dementia enhance the adherence in HAU and its cognitive benefits. In the proposed framework, FSS defines family support as the key external supportive environment, TAM specifies the hearing aids perceptions through which such support is translated into behaviour-related experience, and SDT explains how these supportive experiences are internalised through identification regulation and integration regulation to strengthen autonomous motivation. We therefore hypothesise that family support improves perceived ease of use, perceived compatibility, and perceived observability of hearing aids; these changes facilitate the internalisation of motivation and enhance autonomous motivation; and increased autonomous motivation promotes sustained adherence to HAU, ultimately contributing to improved cognitive and related health outcomes. To date, only one previous study has applied the behavioural change technique of ‘motivational interviewing’ for hearing aid adherence intervention, and it examined HAU hours and self-reported hearing aid effectiveness among new hearing aid users. 23 However, this study did not specifically target older adults at high risk for dementia and did not incorporate intervention strategies from a family support perspective. Although some ongoing RCT protocols also examined the effect of combined HAU and adherence intervention on cognitive function among older adults with MCI, 24 26 they did not conduct any hearing aid interventions for participants in control groups and failed to ascertain the net effect of behavioural interventions on cognitive function and other outcomes. Based on this, the study introduced the design and methods of the family-supported hearing aid use behaviour intervention to improve outcomes in older adults at high risk for dementia (SOUND), which focus on older adults with HL and MCI. This project is an assessor-blinded, parallel-group RCT designed to investigate whether a combined HAU and hearing aid use behaviour intervention guided by SDT-TAM-FSS theory will improve cognitive function and hearing aid adherence relative to only HAU on Chinese older adults with both HL and high dementia risk.

This study is a two-arm, single-blinded, RCT to be conducted in the Department of Otolaryngology, Head and Neck Surgery, Peking University First Hospital in China. Eligible participants will be randomised to either an intervention group (HAU and family intervention) or a control group (HAU and regular health education) in a 1:1 ratio. All participants will undergo baseline assessment conducted by assessors blinded to allocation after screening. Subsequently, participants in the intervention group will receive hearing aid fitting or adjusting by audiologists, along with hearing aid use behaviour intervention by family caregivers under the guidance of researchers whereas participants in the control group will also undergo hearing aid fitting or adjusting, as well as regular health education by audiologists during the follow-up period of 4 months. 2 months and 4 months after inclusion, all participants will undergo follow-up assessments using the same procedure as the baseline assessment. Detailed information on the study design is presented in figure 1 . Our study is scheduled to commence on 6 November 2024 and conclude on 30 November 2026. Recruitment began in November 2024 and is anticipated to conclude by May 2026. The latest protocol (version 1.3) was dated 17 April 2026. At the time of submission (August 2025), a total of 118 participants (60 from intervention groups and 58 from control groups) were recruited and 93 participants (40 from intervention groups and 53 from control groups) have completed baseline and two follow-up visits. Participant recruitment and follow-up are still ongoing as of April 2026.

150 participants aged 60–85 years with MCI and HL will be included in this study. Considering the hearing status of participants, MCI was defined as scoring between 18 and lower than 26 according to the Montreal Cognitive Assessment–Hearing Impairment (MOCA-HI). 26 As for the hearing threshold of the included participants, according to the World Report on Hearing from the WHO, most individuals with mild HL (hearing thresholds of 20 to <35 dB HL) did not need hearing aids, while those with profound HL or above (≥80 dB HL) were more suitable for cochlear implants. 27 Thus, we included participants with moderate to severe HL, and the hearing thresholds were pure-tone average (PTA) of the better ear at 500, 1k, 2k, and 4k Hz was 35–80 dB HL. This hearing threshold is also consistent with a previous study named CHOICE project, which aimed to explore whether the use of hearing aids can enhance cognitive function in older adults diagnosed with age-related HL and MCI. 24 As for the eyesight exclusion criterion, it is used to exclude participants who cannot clearly read the visual instructions of the MOCA-HI. Hence, those with visual acuity better than 20/63 will also be included. Furthermore, this criterion was also consistent with the ARHIEVE programme. 9 Additional inclusion and exclusion criteria are presented in table 1 . Recruitment will be conducted among individuals with age-related HL who are seeking medical services in the outpatient audiology clinics of Peking University First Hospital. Audiologists will also approach participants by a multi-channel approach, such as telephone, posters and text messages. The recruitment process of the trial is as follows. First, audiologists in the outpatient audiology clinics will identify potential individuals with HL who are aged between 60 and 85 years, were new-users or wore hearing aids for less than 3 months, and met the corresponding PTA criteria 24 (see in table 1 ). The hearing threshold is selected following the World Report on Hearing from the WHO, which states that individuals with moderate to severe HL (PTA of the better ear between 35 and 80 dB HL) are suitable for hearing aids. 27 Second, participants will be screened based on the inclusion and exclusion criteria. Third, eligible individuals will then be invited to undergo final in-person assessments of MCI based on MOCA-HI via an online questionnaire conducted by trained audiologists. Informed consent will be signed at enrolment and the Chinese and English versions of the informed consent are shown in online supplemental appendix A . Participants will be finally included if no exclusion criteria are met during in-person assessments and then baseline assessment will be conducted.

After ascertaining eligibility and informed consent, participants will be randomly assigned by an independent research team member who is not involved in data collection or analysis using a computer-generated randomisation sequence. Block randomisation will be employed with the block size of 10 to prevent predictability. Participants will be informed of their allocation after randomisation but will not be aware of the details of each group. Given that participants in the control group will not receive hearing aid use behaviour intervention by family caregivers, blinding of participants is not feasible. However, assessors will be blinded to the allocation, and participants will be requested not to disclose allocation to assessors at any time during the study.

The intervention of HAU is delivered by professional audiologists in the outpatient audiology clinics, which is performed on participants among both intervention and control groups. The family-supported hearing aid use behaviour intervention (family intervention, FI) is developed based on SDT-TAM-FSS theory, which is delivered by family caregivers at home after receiving 1 hour training from the researchers and will be guided using two manuals: HL knowledge and HAU manual, and hearing rehabilitation and family intervention manual. The family intervention is performed on participants in the intervention group, who are further guided through a WeChat (Tencent) group established by audiologists and researchers to address unresolved issues concerning hearing aid maintenance and family intervention skills.

sections.section: Hau And Family-Supported Hearing Aid Use Behaviour Intervention (Intervention Group)
sections.text: Participants allocated to the intervention group will receive bilateral hearing aids without restrictions on brand or type, based on their degree of HL, cognitive function, and personal preferences. Hearing aids will be fitted and adjusted by audiologists in outpatient audiology clinics. In addition, participants will undergo a family-empowered intervention to improve adherence to HAU, consisting of three components ( table 2 ).

This component involves a 1 hour face-to-face interactive training lesson as well as a booster training lesson via WeChat (Tencent) group delivered by researchers to participants and their caregivers, supported by accessible teaching materials, such as training manuals and slides. The lesson includes 40 min of structured teaching and 20 min of interactive Q&A. The content covers HL knowledge, HAU skills and autonomous motivation analysis for HAU. It also provides for family caregivers on how to provide autonomous motivation support. The training aims to identify barriers to autonomous motivation and to improve awareness of hearing care among both participants and caregivers. Detailed contents of the standardised training manuals are titled as ‘Steps before family-supported intervention’, ‘Steps during family-supported intervention’ and ‘Steps for providing feedback during intervention’. Booster training materials will be delivered regularly via WeChat group.

This component is delivered by family caregivers at home over a 4-month period. Caregivers are trained to recognise different usage scenarios and to provide personalised support based on the manuals. Key procedures generally include understanding opinions, sharing experiences, setting plans and goals and solving difficulties during implementation. The aim is to promote the development of consistent HAU habits and enhance autonomous motivation.

Ongoing support is provided through the WeChat (Tencent) group established by audiologists and researchers. Caregivers can seek assistance for unresolved issues related to HAU and maintenance during the process of family intervention. Besides, caregivers complete weekly patient-reported outcomes (PROs), including duration and frequency of HAU and any discomfort experienced. In order to reduce the caregiver burden, some strategies will be implemented. On the one hand, researchers have divided training procedures into steps and the language of the training manual is simple and easy to understand, which reduces the burden of understanding manual content for caregivers. On the other hand, researchers will keep a close eye on the data from weekly patient-reported questionnaires and proactively assist caregivers in resolving issues during the intervention process within WeChat group, rather than waiting for the feedback from caregivers.

sections.section: Hau And Regular Health Education (Control Group)
sections.text: Participants in the control group will also receive bilateral hearing aids and the procedure is consistent with those among the intervention group. In addition, participants will undergo regular health education during the hearing aid fitting, which contains prevention on HL, basic HAU skills and brief introduction to hearing aid functions. However, the corresponding content is different from that in the intervention group in terms of specific content and implementation methods, which reduce the risk of contamination. On the one hand, participants in the control group will receive basic knowledge and skills on HAU irrelevant to their type of hearing aids while those in the intervention group will receive knowledge and skills on HAU corresponding to their uncomfortable circumstances of HAU through Q&A process during the face-to-face training lesson along with the WeChat group. On the other hand, the relevant knowledge and skills are verbally informed to participants from the control group whereas those are provided through HL knowledge and HAU manual in the intervention group.

sections.section: Implementation Of Family-Supported Hearing Aid Use Behaviour Intervention Guided By Sdt-Tam-Fss Theory
sections.text: As stated above, the family-supported hearing aid use behaviour intervention is guided by the SDT-TAM-FSS theory, which is presented in figure 2 . Within this framework, SDT provides the core mechanism by explaining how supportive external environments facilitate identification regulation and integration regulation, thereby strengthening autonomous motivation and promoting sustained HAU. 21 FSS contextualises external supportive environmental factors on family support by emphasising the role of family caregivers as a primary source of support. It divides family support into three categories including emotional support (listening, comforting and understanding from family caregivers), instrumental support (material resources, financial support and specific guidance and demonstration from family caregivers) and informative support (praise and affirmation from family caregivers), 28 which together provide a personalised, interactive and sustainable support system for older adults. TAM complements these theories by identifying key perceptual factors that influence behavioural adoption, including perceived ease of use (the difficulties), perceived compatibility (the degree of comfort after HAU) and perceived observability of hearing aids (the effectiveness perceived after HAU). 22 However, the TAM-related constructs in the SDT-TAM-FSS framework are not prespecified primary or secondary outcomes in this trial. Instead, they are used to inform intervention design, and only related process information will be descriptively captured through existing study measures. For example, family caregivers can enhance perceived observability of older adults by conveying praise or affirmation to them, further stimulating autonomous motivation of HAU through identification regulation. Thus, a higher level of autonomous motivation could help them enhance the adherence of HAU and its cognitive benefits. It is also noteworthy that the SDT-TAM-FSS framework proposes a sequential behavioural pathway rather than three independent theoretical components. In this model, family support, as conceptualised by FSS, serves as the primary external supportive environment. This support is hypothesised to influence HAU first through TAM-related perceptual factors, including perceived ease of use, perceived compatibility and perceived observability. Improvements in these perceptions are then expected to facilitate internalisation of motivation through identification regulation and integration regulation, as described by SDT, thereby strengthening autonomous motivation for HAU. Enhanced autonomous motivation is in turn expected to improve adherence to HAU, which may subsequently lead to better cognitive function and other health outcomes. The SDT-TAM-FSS framework is operationalised across the three components of the intervention. For instance, in the cognitive restructuring component, HL knowledge and HAU skills training are informed by TAM to improve perceived ease of use and compatibility. Autonomous motivation analysis is grounded in SDT to specify the motivation types. Training on key points of providing autonomous motivation support is based on FSS, aiming to improve instrumental and informative support from family caregivers. Detailed mappings between theoretical constructs and intervention components are presented in table 2 . The integrated framework explains more than any single theory by specifying how family support is translated into sustained HAU through perceptual and motivational mechanisms. FSS identifies the source of support, TAM specifies the proximal perception-related pathways, and SDT explains how these experiences are internalised into autonomous motivation that supports long-term adherence.

Evaluation of the following outcomes will take place at the screening, baseline assessment and follow-up visits at 2 and 4 months after the intervention. Each assessment will follow the same sequence to minimise the differences between participants. Detailed outcomes are listed in table 3 .

The primary outcome is cognitive function, which will be measured by the MOCA-HI. 29 This scale was specially designed for individuals with HL with the substitution of verbal instructions with visual instructions, considering that test performances of the origin version of MOCA are negatively impacted even if degree of HL is not severe enough to prohibit standard verbal administration of the test. 30 MOCA-HI contains executive function, language, orientation, calculations, conceptual thinking, memory, visuoperception, attention and concentration and participants with 12 years or fewer of formal education will be added 2 points if they have a score of less than or equal to 28, thus leading to a possible maximum of 30 points. 31 In addition, MOCA-HI has validated cut-off points for the identification of MCI and participants scored above 18 and below 26 are considered to have MCI. 26 31

Secondary outcomes will include adherence score of HAU (measured by daily duration and weekly frequency), 32 Hearing Handicap Inventory for the Elderly-Screening Version (HHIE-S), 33 34 International Outcome Inventory for Hearing Aids (IOI-HA), 35 36 Practical Hearing Aid Skills Test (PHAST), 37 Treatment Self-Regulation Questionnaire, 38 39 activities of daily living (ADL), Quality of Life EuroQol-5D-5L (EQ-5D-5L), 40 Geriatric Depression Scale-15 (GDS-15), 41 Subjective Cognitive Decline Questionnaire (SCD-Q9), 42 43 social support, 44 the General Self-Efficacy Scale, 45 healthcare utilisation, intervention cost, Autonomy Support Scale, 46 and caregiver burden. Social support will be assessed by Lubben Social Network Scale whereas caregiver burden will be evaluated by Zarit Burden Interview. 47 According to a previous study, 48 intervention cost will cover purchase and maintenance costs of hearing aids. Among the secondary outcomes, adherence score of HAU, HHIE-S, IOI-HA, HAU skills, motivation of HAU and autonomy motivation support are key secondary measures and ADL, quality of life, depressive symptoms, SCD-Q9, social support, self-efficacy, healthcare utilisation, intervention cost and caregiver burden are exploratory secondary outcomes.
A comprehensive process evaluation will be undertaken to assess the quality of family intervention implementation and its potential effects on study outcomes across multiple dimensions.
We will track and document eligibility, recruitment and retention rates, as well as reasons why participants withdraw from the study.

Data on intervention acceptability will be collected through continuing weekly PRO questionnaire for caregivers. Number of times caregivers submit weekly PRO questionnaires will be calculated. Furthermore, dropouts will be defined as failing to submit weekly PRO questionnaires for two consecutive weeks. Dropped-out participants will be encouraged to complete the follow-up measurements.
Outcome acceptability will be assessed by rates of outcome questionnaire completion at baseline, 2 months and 4 months.

Adverse events will include any worsening of underlying diseases or new-onset hearing system abnormalities. All events will be recorded in the electronic database, with serious adverse events promptly reported to the appropriate authorities.

In the study design, the adherence on HAU will be used to monitor fidelity. To be specific, the duration and frequency of HAU will be asked in the baseline assessment as well as the weekly PROs. Researchers will compare the data between baseline assessment and weekly questionnaires. In the caregiver training, fidelity will be monitored by standard training procedures and booster training sessions. The slides and contents of standardised training manuals will also be sent to WeChat group regularly to minimise ‘drift’ in training skills. In the delivery and receipt of treatment, fidelity will be monitored by asking caregivers questions when conducting the 1-hour, interactive, and face-to-face training lesson. The lesson will last for 40 min, and interactive Q&A will last for 20 min. Researchers will ask caregivers questions relevant to HAU skills and key points of providing autonomous motivation support to maintain that family caregivers can understand training lessons. Furthermore, family caregivers are free to raise questions during the face-to-face training lesson. In the enactment of treatment skills, fidelity will be monitored by audiotape record when conducting the 2-month and 4-month follow-up. For instance, when conducting the PHAST, assessors will ask participants where they learnt this knowledge and skills. Then researchers will listen to the recordings to determine whether participants learn the skills from training manuals.

This study follows Good Clinical Practice guidelines for RCTs. Data collection will be conducted by assessors who are blinded to the allocation through structured electronic questionnaire. Assessors will be trained through the standard operating procedures protocol manual from the research team prior to data collection, and then conduct face-to-face interviews with each eligible participant. The last four digits of the identity card of each participant will be assigned as a unique ID account and other personal identification information will not be collected. All data and information collected during the trial will be kept strictly confidential and only be used for research purposes. The findings of this trial will be reported according to the revised Consolidated Standards of Reporting Trials (CONSORT) guidelines. The protocol is written following the Standard Protocol Items: Recommendations for Interventional Trials reporting guidelines 49 and in the Template for Intervention Description and Replication format. 50

The sample size calculation is based on the effect sizes for the primary outcome of cognitive function in two previous studies, leading to the effect size ranging from 0.58 to 0.75. 51 52 This study estimates sample size based on the conservative ES of 0.58. Assuming a risk of type I error (α) of 5%, a power (1−β) of 90%, the required sample size for each group is 64. Meanwhile, considering a 15% dropout rate in the follow-up, we aim to recruit 75 per arm for a total of 150 participants (1:1 ratio). The sample size was calculated using G*power (V.3.1.9.7). All analyses will follow CONSORT guidelines. Mean and SD or median and IQR will be used to describe continuous demographic and baseline characteristics of both intervention and control groups, considering normality of the data, whereas number and percentage for categorical data. Unpaired t-test or one-way analysis of variance and χ² test will be used to compare the features between intervention and control groups, and paired t-test will be used to conduct within-group comparisons. Non-parametric tests will be used to compare data that do not follow a normal distribution. The intent-to-treat principle will be used to examine the effect of family intervention of hearing aid adherence on all primary and secondary outcomes and the last observation carried forward will be utilised for handling missing data. Exploratory analyses will also be conducted using per-protocol analyses for all outcomes, including all participants adhering to the specified intervention protocol with baseline and 4-month outcome data available to assess optimal efficacy under ideal conditions. Difference-in-difference will be conducted to compare the changes in primary outcome over time between the HAU and FI intervention along with control groups, both before and after the intervention, thus identifying the significance and effect size of the family intervention. Besides, linear mixed-effects and analysis of covariance model will be employed to analyse the secondary outcomes at 2 months and 4 months, considering covariates such as age, sex, educational level, marital status, etc. Heterogeneity analysis of different levels of adherence to the intervention (measured by number of times caregivers submit weekly PRO questionnaires) will be conducted. Interim analysis will also be conducted under strict confidentiality by the principal investigator when all subjects completed the 2-month follow-up assessment using data from baseline and follow-up visit at 2 months after the intervention. The purpose of interim analysis is to facilitate early dissemination of results for the study’s primary outcome. Health economic analyses will include cost-effectiveness analysis and cost–utility analysis. The former will integrate intervention costs and outcomes to calculate the incremental cost-effectiveness ratio and the latter will integrate intervention costs and health state utility (measured by EQ-5D-5L) to calculate incremental cost–utility ratio. All statistical tests will be two-tailed, with a significance level set at p<0.05. All analyses will be conducted using Stata SE V.17.0.

To the best of our knowledge, the SOUND programme is the first RCT worldwide which aims to examine the efficacy of hearing aid use behaviour intervention on cognitive function among older adults with HL and high dementia risk in the context of family-supported and based on the integrated health behaviour theory of SDT-TAM-FSS. This protocol specifies the design and rationale of family-supported hearing aid use behaviour intervention study. One previous RCT evaluated the effect of adherence intervention via motivational interviewing on HAU hours among new hearing aid users, compared with standard in-person audiological care. 23 However, this trial recruited participants without dementia risk and failed to include cognitive outcomes. Besides, several previous RCTs, such as CHOICE programme, 24 HearCog programme 26 and TACT programme, 53 have performed HAU and adherence intervention on older adults with both HL and high dementia risk, and some of them have revealed that the above interventions exerted significant effect on specific cognitive function domains as well as daily HAU duration. 26 53 However, they failed to examine the net effect of adherence intervention on cognitive function given that participants in the control group did not receive hearing aid fitting. Hence, our SOUND programme will provide high-level evidence for the cognitive benefits of HAU along with the hearing aid use behaviour intervention for HL older adults with high dementia risk. Furthermore, the above RCT using motivational interviewing technique requires efforts from practicing therapists and fails to introduce behaviour theories when conducting motivational interviewing. 23 Thus, our SOUND programme will also enhance the participation of family caregivers and expand the application scope of health behaviour theory of SDT-TAM-FSS to HAU behaviour. Additionally, a systematic review on factors for HAU among people with dementia and HL indicated that family members’ supportive and encouraging attitudes towards HAU are one of the most important factors for HAU. 54 Thus, compared with other theory-driven behaviour intervention on sound amplification device use delivered by community health workers, 55 family-supported hearing aid use behaviour intervention that stimulates the autonomous motivation of HAU in our study serves as an evidence-based approach for dementia prevention and is more feasible in places with scarce specialist resources. Moreover, the follow-up period of our study is 4 months, which is consistent with another previous cross-national RCT named SENSE-Cog programme, 56 which aimed to examine the clinical impact of hearing aid rehabilitation and support among people with mild-to-moderate dementia and concurrent hearing difficulties, especially that conducted in the Asian country of Pakistan. 57 The 2-month and 4-month window is also adequate to assess hearing aid use adherence considering that a previous study demonstrated a significantly greater HAU adherence among first-time hearing aid users after only 6-week behaviour intervention. 58 Besides, our 2-month and 4-month window to measure hearing aid adherence is also similar to a previous RCT aiming to evaluate the effect of adherence intervention via motivational interviewing on HAU hours among new hearing aid users over 1-month and 3-month follow-up visits. 23 There are also several limitations. First, a potential limitation of the SOUND programme is its restricted accessibility, as it can only be implemented for individuals who have support from family caregivers and possess internet or digital device access. Second, it is impossible to blind subjects to their receipt of the intervention due to the intervention characteristics in the control group. However, assessors will be blinded to the allocation, and participants will be requested not to disclose allocation to assessors at any time during the study. Third, since our assessment of cognitive function and hearing use adherence score is based on self-reports, there is a risk of measurement bias. To mitigate this, we will employ validated instruments, conduct cross-validation, and incorporate evaluations from multiple sources. Fourth, although some evidence has suggested that significant cognitive benefits of HAU were found during 3 month period, 59 60 the comparatively shorter follow-up time of 4 months might limit the detection of cognitive change. Studies containing longer follow-up periods will be conducted in the future. Fifth, despite that researchers will make sure that the caregivers understand the intervention procedures in the standardised training manuals via interactive and face-to-face training lessons, the absence of information on the competence of family caregivers may bring about hindrance for family caregivers to deliver aspects of the intervention. Sixth, there is an absence of patient and public involvement planned for our study, which weakens the applicability of the conclusions. Sixth, the TAM-related constructs were not assessed using dedicated validated instruments. Therefore, although the SDT-TAM-FSS framework informed intervention design, the present trial is not intended to provide a formal test of the underlying theoretical mechanism. To conclude, our SOUND programme will provide high-level evidence on how family-supported intervention affects cognitive function through adherence on HAU and autonomous motivation among older adults with HL and high risk for dementia. Results from this study will help enhance the role of family caregivers in the prevention of dementia by demonstrating how caregivers can participate in daily hearing management, motivate regular use, and help address common barriers that lead to poor adherence on hearing aids. The intervention framework may also be adopted by community and primary care services as a low-resource model that does not require intensive involvement of audiology specialists. Furthermore, the results may guide policy efforts to integrate caregiver training and hearing aid adherence monitoring into broader dementia-prevention strategies and involve multiple stakeholders including communities, families and hospitals. Finally, the study will advance behavioural science by providing empirical evidence on how constructs derived from SDT, TAM and FSS can predict adherence patterns in hearing rehabilitation.
